intro: This guide walks a Sunday school class, homeschool group or family through “Talks to the Farmer (For Children)” in twelve weeks, one chapter a week. Each chapter takes one picture from the farming year — a weedy field, a sower, the first green shoot, sheep at shearing, the harvest — and shows what it teaches about God. It works for a small family around the table or a class of up to twenty, and is best for ages 6–12.

Each session takes about 30 minutes. Welcome everyone and say the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter aloud (5–7 minutes). Talk together using the chapter’s three questions (5–10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or your own (2 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter yourself beforehand and have paper, pencils and crayons ready; the activities use simple farm and nature ideas, and no real soil, seeds or plants are needed. A few chapters touch on sad or hard things — losing something we love, hard times, and going home to God at the end — so read them gently, let children say as much or as little as they want, and keep coming back to the book’s own comfort: God is the kind farmer who cares for every plant in his field.

weeks.summary: King Solomon walks past a lazy man’s field and finds it covered in weeds and thistles. The man never planted a single weed; he simply did nothing, and a field never stays empty — if good plants are not grown, weeds come all by themselves. Our hearts are the same, so we should plant good seeds like a kind word or a little prayer today, not “tomorrow.” The big idea: doing good is something we start now, because doing nothing lets bad things grow on their own.

memory_verse.text: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise.

activity.title: Weed or Wheat?
steps: Have everyone stand in a space with room to move: you are all a farmer’s field.
Call out everyday things one at a time, such as “saying sorry,” “a kind word,” “a grumpy face,” “saying a prayer,” “saying ‘I’ll do it tomorrow.’”
For a good seed, stretch up tall like wheat; for a weed, crouch low and wiggle your fingers like a thistle.
After a few rounds, let children take turns calling out good seeds and weeds for the group to sort.
Finish standing tall, and each say one good seed you will plant today.

weeks.summary: Solomon looks again at the lazy man’s farm and sees that its stone wall has fallen down. Each time a stone fell out the man said, “I’ll fix it tomorrow,” so sheep and goats got in, weeds blew in and the rain washed the soil away. Our hearts have a wall too, made of saying our prayers, listening to those who teach us about God, and being brave enough to say “no” to wrong. The big idea: keep the wall strong, and if a stone falls out, just put one stone back.

memory_verse.text: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.

activity.title: My Strong Stone Wall
steps: Draw a little field in the middle of your paper with good plants growing in it.
Draw a stone wall all the way around it, with big stones.
In three of the stones write or draw the good things from the chapter: praying, listening to people who teach you about God, and saying “no” to wrong.
Fill the other stones with good things of your own, then show your wall to a neighbour.

weeks.summary: On a frosty morning everything is hard and frozen, but a warm wind blows, the sun comes out, and the ice melts away — and the Bible says God sends both the frost and the warm wind. When we do wrong, our hearts can feel cold and sorry like frost, but when we tell God we are sorry, his love melts the sadness and he forgives us. Only God can melt a heart like that. The big idea: don’t stay frozen — tell God you are sorry, and he loves to forgive.

memory_verse.text: He sends out his word, and melts them. He causes his wind to blow, and the waters flow.

activity.title: Frozen and Melted
steps: Explain the game: when you say “Frost!” everyone freezes stiff like ice, and when you say “Warm wind!” everyone slowly melts down to the floor.
Play a few rounds, sometimes quickly and sometimes slowly, so everyone listens carefully.
On the last round, after melting, have everyone stand up slowly and stretch out their arms like the sunshine.
Say together, “God melts our hearts with his love,” then say the memory verse.

weeks.summary: One seed kept safe in a jar stays one seed forever, but a seed planted in the ground splits open and grows into a tall plant with many new seeds. Jesus said he was like that seed: he gave his life, and because he did, many, many people can have new life with God. We can be like that too: holding everything for ourselves keeps us small, but giving and sharing makes our lives grow. Jesus giving his life is told very gently here; keep it as simple as the chapter does. The big idea: giving is not losing — giving is how good things grow.

memory_verse.text: Most assuredly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.

activity.title: One Seed, Many Seeds
steps: Fold your paper in half.
On one side, draw a jar on a shelf with just one lonely seed inside it.
On the other side, draw a seed in the ground growing up into a tall plant covered with lots of new seeds.
Next to some of the new seeds, write or draw a way you could give or share this week.
Write “Giving is not losing” across the bottom.

weeks.summary: Jesus tells of a farmer scattering seed: some falls on the hard path and the birds eat it, some on rocky ground and dries up, some among thorns and gets crowded out, and some on good soil and grows into a big harvest. The seed is God’s word, and the kinds of ground are like kinds of hearts. Even hard ground can be dug up and made soft, and God will get our hearts ready if we ask him. The big idea: ask God to make your heart like good soil, ready to listen and grow.

memory_verse.text: That in the good ground, these are such as in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and bring forth fruit with patience.

activity.title: The Sower’s Seeds with Actions
steps: Teach an action for each place the seeds land: flapping arms for the birds on the hard path, fanning your face for the hot sun on rocky ground, squeezing in tight for the crowding weeds, and growing up tall for the good soil.
Retell the story slowly while everyone does the actions at the right moment.
Tell it a second time and let the children call out what happens next before they do each action.
Finish with everyone growing up tall, and pray together, “God, make my heart good soil.”

weeks.summary: After winter the ground looks bare, but in spring a tiny green shoot pushes up through the soil — so small you could step on it, but alive, and the beginning of a whole field of wheat. Loving God can start small like that, with a little prayer or a little faith, and God sees it and is very happy. A good farmer never stamps on a little shoot but waters it and helps it grow, and that is what God does with us. The big idea: no love for God is too small to count, and God helps it grow.

memory_verse.text: You drench its furrows. You level its ridges. You soften it with showers. You bless it with a crop.

activity.title: From Shoot to Wheat
steps: Fold your paper in half and then in half again, then open it to show four boxes.
In the first box draw brown, bare winter ground; in the second, one tiny green shoot poking up.
In the third box draw the plant growing taller, with the sun shining and rain falling on it.
In the fourth box draw tall golden wheat, and write underneath, “God helps me grow.”

weeks.summary: Once a year the farmer shears his sheep’s heavy wool so they stay cool in summer. A wise sheep lies still and is never hurt; it is the kicking and wriggling that hurts, not the shears. Sometimes God takes away something we love, but he chooses the right time, he always has something good to give, like wool growing back, and it hurts least when we stay still and trust him — as Jesus stayed quiet and gentle when people were unkind to him. Some children may think of real losses; let them share only if they want to. The big idea: when hard things happen, we can be still and trust God, because he loves us.

memory_verse.text: Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations. I will be exalted in the earth.

activity.title: Still as a Sheep
steps: Have everyone sit or lie down comfortably, like sheep at shearing time.
Challenge the group to stay completely still and quiet for thirty seconds while you walk quietly around; then try a whole minute.
Ask: was it easy or hard to stay still? Talk about how the wise sheep stays still because it trusts the farmer.
Stay still once more while you slowly say the memory verse, then have everyone say it together in a whisper.

weeks.summary: Grass grows everywhere and we hardly notice it, but God makes every blade grow, and he grows it for the cows and sheep, who cannot even say thank you. Every blade gets its own drop of dew in the morning, which shows how carefully God gives each thing what it needs. If God takes such care of grass and animals, how much more does he care for us. The big idea: God sees you, knows what you need and has never once forgotten you.

memory_verse.text: He causes the grass to grow for the cattle, and plants for man to cultivate, that he may bring forth food out of the earth.

activity.title: God Takes Care Of…
steps: Sit in a circle.
Start by saying, “God takes care of the grass.”
The next person repeats it and adds one more thing, such as “God takes care of the grass and the cows.”
Keep going round, each person repeating the list and adding one thing, and help anyone who gets stuck.
When the list is long, finish all together with, “…and God takes care of me!”

weeks.summary: All summer the farmer plants, weeds and waits, and at last comes harvest: the grain is gathered, the barn is full and everyone celebrates with a feast. The Bible says God’s people have happy times like harvest, and the happiest is when someone comes to love God; Spurgeon said helping one person know Jesus made him happier than all the treasure in the world. A farmer’s rule is worth knowing: you grow what you plant. The big idea: plant kindness, prayers and love for God now, and God will grow a happy harvest.

memory_verse.text: Let us not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up.

activity.title: My Seed Packet
steps: Fold your paper in half to make a seed packet.
On the front, write the name of a good thing to plant, such as “Kindness Seeds” or “Prayer Seeds,” and decorate it.
On the inside, draw what it will grow into, like a happy friend, a helped neighbour or a heart full of love for God.
On the back, write “Planting instructions”: one thing you will do this week to plant it.
Show your packet to a neighbour and take it home.

weeks.summary: Ruth was poor, so she gleaned, bending again and again to pick up the bits of grain the workers dropped. Boaz, who owned the field, quietly told his workers to drop extra grain on purpose where she would find it and to be kind to her, and he never told her he had done it. God is like kind Boaz: he has many good things for us, and we gather them by coming to him, listening and praying; and like Ruth, who took food home to share, we can share God’s gifts with others. The big idea: God is generous to us, so we can be generous too.

memory_verse.text: Also pull out some for her from the bundles, and leave it, and let her glean, and don’t rebuke her.

activity.title: Gathering Grain for Ruth
activity.materials: Small torn scraps of paper prepared by the leader, and a pencil
steps: Before the session, tear paper into small “grains” (at least two per child) and write a kind or encouraging word on each, such as “You are loved” or “God sees you.”
While the children wait outside the room or close their eyes, scatter the grains around the room, “dropped on purpose,” like Boaz’s workers did.
Let everyone gently gather grains until each child has at least two.
Read your grains, then give one away to someone else in the group, just as Ruth shared what she gathered.

weeks.summary: Each grain of wheat is stuck inside a hard husk, so the farmer beats it with a stick to set the good grain free; this is threshing, and it is not unkind. Hard or sad times can feel a little like that, but the farmer only threshes the good grain, never the weeds, so a hard time does not mean God has forgotten us; and he never beats the grain forever, so hard times do not last forever either. Some children may be in a hard time now; reassure them, and don’t ask anyone to name their troubles aloud. The big idea: in hard times we are still precious to God, and the hard times will end.

memory_verse.text: For the needy shall not always be forgotten, nor the hope of the poor perish forever.

activity.title: Precious Grain Card
steps: Clap together “bang, bang, bang” like the farmer threshing, then stop suddenly and say, “The farmer always stops!” Do this two or three times.
Fold a sheet of paper in half to make a card.
On the front, draw a tall, golden ear of wheat full of grains.
Inside, write “I am precious to God, and hard times don’t last forever.”
Take the card home and keep it somewhere you will see it on a hard day.

weeks.summary: The very last part of the harvest is the happiest: the good wheat is carried safely into the barn, where no rain, frost or wind can hurt it. Jesus said one day God will gather all his people from every country, big and small, young and old, safely home to be with him in heaven, where there is no more crying or sadness. For everyone who loves God, the end is not something to fear; it is going home, and anyone can tell God they want to belong to him. Some children may think of someone who has died; answer gently, and let them share only if they wish. The big idea: God gathers his people safely home, and we can belong to him.

memory_verse.text: In my Father’s house are many mansions. If it weren’t so, I would have told you. I am going to prepare a place for you.

activity.title: Everyone in the Barn
activity.materials: A large sheet of paper (or several sheets laid side by side) and crayons
steps: Draw a big, warm barn on the large sheet together, with the doors wide open.
Have each child draw a bundle of golden wheat inside the barn and write their name on it.
Add more wheat bundles for people from all over the world, big and small, young and old.
Write “Gathered safely home” across the top, and pray together, thanking God that his people belong to him.
